html:
On the headset problem that @dizzarz raised: you could use a CAVE (cave automatic virtual environment).

Projectors throw the images onto several large screens, and people can walk around freely inside or adjust their position in space with a controller. The interactivity and immersion are far beyond a headset, and the sound experience (auralization) in particular is much more realistic. With a headset, sound can currently only be played back over headphones, which produces in-head localization: the sound always seems to come from inside your own head, and this gets worse when the head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) aren’t measured individually. A CAVE offers two audio options, headphones or loudspeakers. Loudspeaker playback solves the in-head problem but needs special filters to cancel crosstalk and room reverberation; with them, you get spatial audio that is tracked and updated in real time. What it can’t yet handle is real-time interaction between several people.

Besides, VR applications today are far too narrow. The industry focuses only on games and entertainment, and only on vision, while the other senses tend to be ignored. Then again, that matches what people expect of VR: if what you see doesn’t look real, how is anyone supposed to believe in it? I remember that at the 2015 Hannover Messe there was already a whole hall devoted to VR, and many companies presented applications that were forward-looking then and still are today: training for hazardous operations, distance learning, remote guidance (which also involves AR), interior design, architectural design and more. I work in acoustics, and there’s plenty of scope for applications there too: noise prediction, concert hall design, acoustics in urban planning, traffic noise and so on. This is exactly what the top acoustics institutes in Europe are all pouring money and effort into. So broaden your horizons, or the industry will dig its own grave.
